guide.title: Period 6 (1865–1898): review guide
guide.intro: After the Civil War, the United States became an industrial power. Railroads, corporations, and immigrants transformed the economy and cities, the West was settled at great cost to American Indians, and Americans argued over what role government should play.

sections.title: The West, American Indians, and the New South
body: Transcontinental railroads (the first completed in 1869), the Homestead Act, mining, and cattle ranching drew settlers west. The federal government confined American Indians to reservations, fought wars against nations such as the Lakota and Nez Perce, and through the Dawes Act (1887) broke up communal lands and pushed assimilation. Some American Indians resisted, including through the Ghost Dance movement.

Boosters of a “New South” called for industry and railroads, but most Southerners remained farmers, and many Black and poor white families were trapped in sharecropping and debt. Southern states passed segregation (Jim Crow) laws, upheld in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), and disfranchised Black voters.
points: Contextualization: western settlement depended on federal land policy and railroads.
The New South's industrial promise was only partly realized.

sections.title: Industrial capitalism and labor
body: Technological innovation (steel, electricity, the telephone) and new business methods created huge corporations. Andrew Carnegie (steel) used vertical integration; John D. Rockefeller (oil) used horizontal integration and trusts. Defenders invoked laissez-faire, Social Darwinism, and the Gospel of Wealth.

Industrial workers faced long hours, dangerous conditions, and low wages. They organized in the Knights of Labor and the American Federation of Labor, and strikes such as the Great Railroad Strike (1877), Homestead (1892), and Pullman (1894) were often broken with government help. A growing middle class of managers and clerks enjoyed new consumer goods and leisure.
points: Government usually sided with employers in major strikes.

sections.title: Immigration, reform, and politics
body: “New immigrants” from southern and eastern Europe and from Asia filled growing cities; nativists pushed back, and the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) barred most Chinese immigration. Reformers such as Jane Addams founded settlement houses, and the Pendleton Act (1883) began civil service reform.

Farmers squeezed by falling crop prices, debt, and railroad rates formed the Grange and then the Populist (People's) Party, whose Omaha Platform (1892) demanded government regulation, a graduated income tax, and free coinage of silver. William Jennings Bryan carried free silver into the 1896 election and lost to William McKinley. Continuity and change: debates about government's role in the economy carried into the Progressive Era.
points: Populists wanted more government action, not less.
Free silver aimed to inflate prices and ease farmers' debts.

example.prompt: Explain why many farmers supported free coinage of silver in the 1890s.
example.solution: Farmers faced falling crop prices and heavy debts. Coining silver freely would expand the money supply, raise prices, and make debts easier to pay back, so indebted farmers favored it over the gold standard.

misconceptions: “The West was settled by individuals without government help.”
Federal land grants, railroads, and the army were central.
“Government stayed out of the economy entirely.”
It subsidized railroads and often helped break strikes, while regulating little.
Their core was indebted farmers in the South and West.
“The Dawes Act protected American Indian land.”
It broke up reservations and led to large losses of land.

passages.title: Source A: William Jennings Bryan, speech to the Democratic National Convention, 1896
text: “We say to you that you have made the definition of a business man too limited in its application. The man who is employed for wages is as much a business man as his employer; the attorney in a country town is as much a business man as the corporation counsel in a great metropolis; the merchant at the cross-roads store is as much a business man as the merchant of New York; the farmer who goes forth in the morning and toils all day, who begins in spring and toils all summer, and who by the application of brain and muscle to the natural resources of the country creates wealth, is as much a business man as the man who goes upon the Board of Trade and bets upon the price of grain; . . . We come to speak of this broader class of business men.”
passages.attribution: William Jennings Bryan, speech to the Democratic National Convention in Chicago (the “Cross of Gold” speech), July 1896. Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax U.S. History, section 20.4.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (published before 1931, or a work of the U.S. government). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax U.S. History (openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/20-4-social-and-labor-unrest-in-the-1890s); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source B: Chief Joseph of the Nez Perce, 1877
text: “Tell General Howard I know his heart. What he told me before, I have it in my heart. I am tired of fighting. Our Chiefs are killed. . . . It is cold, and we have no blankets; the little children are freezing to death. My people, some of them, have run away to the hills, and have no blankets, no food. No one knows where they are—perhaps freezing to death. I want to have time to look for my children, and see how many of them I can find. . . . Hear me, my Chiefs! I am tired; my heart is sick and sad. From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever.”
passages.attribution: Words attributed to Chief Joseph of the Nez Perce at his surrender to the U.S. Army near the Canadian border, October 1877, as recorded by U.S. Army officers. Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax U.S. History, section 17.4.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (published before 1931, or a work of the U.S. government). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax U.S. History (openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/17-4-the-assault-on-american-indian-life-and-culture); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source C: An interpretation of industrial capitalism
text: “The industrial economy of the late nineteenth century produced astonishing wealth and astonishing inequality. Steel output soared as Andrew Carnegie controlled every stage of production, from iron mines to rail mills, while Standard Oil came to control most of the nation's oil refining. Workers who made this growth possible often labored twelve hours a day in dangerous conditions. When they struck, as at Homestead in 1892 and Pullman in 1894, employers frequently called on private guards, state militias, or federal troops, and the strikes failed.”
passages.attribution: Interpretation written for StudySprint by its editors. It summarizes widely held historical views and is not a quotation from any published historian.
passages.licenseOrRights: Original text written for StudySprint; it is not taken or adapted from any College Board exam.

passages.title: Source D: An interpretation of immigration and the city
text: “Between 1880 and 1900, millions of immigrants arrived, increasingly from southern and eastern Europe. Most settled in cities, where they found work in factories and built churches, synagogues, newspapers, and mutual-aid societies. Political machines traded jobs and favors for their votes. Many native-born Americans responded with suspicion: nativist organizations warned against Catholics and newcomers, and Congress in 1882 barred most immigration from China. The question of who could become an American was reopened with every arriving ship.”

questions.prompt: Bryan's main purpose in the excerpt is to
choices: argue against government regulation of railroads and banks
defend the gold standard against those who want free silver
claim that workers and farmers matter to the economy as much as wealthy financiers
praise speculators on the Board of Trade for creating the nation's wealth and jobs
questions.explanation: He insists that wage earners, small merchants, and farmers are “as much a business man” as big-city financiers.
choiceExplanations: His supporters wanted more government regulation, not less.
He was the leading opponent of the gold standard.
He contrasts honest work with betting on grain prices.
